Getting Started: Loading the Dataset

Before you begin the practical, you need to load the required dataset into R. To ensure a smooth workflow, please follow one of the two options below:

Option 1: Using a Dedicated Folder

Create a specific folder for this assignment and place the dataset file inside it. You can then load the data using the load() function by specifying the correct file path. (Note for Windows users: Please ensure you change all backslashes \ in your copied file path to forward slashes / in R).

   For Mac users, your path will look like this:

load("/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

   For Windows users, your path will look like this:

load("C:/Users/your_username/Documents/folder_name/dataset_name.RData")

Option 2: Using an R Project

Create an R Project (.Rproj) for this assignment and store the dataset directly within that project folder. Make sure to open RStudio by double-clicking the .Rproj file. This automatically sets your working directory, allowing you to load the dataset directly without a long path:

load("dataset_name.RData")

Note for this specific lab: Please ensure you have downloaded the tumor.Rdata file from the course environment before proceeding.

In this lab we train models to classify tumors as benign (B) or malignant (M).

  • Benign (B): non-cancerous tumors that do not spread to other tissues.
  • Malignant (M): cancerous tumors that can grow aggressively and spread.

The dataset tumor.Rdata contains 569 observations. The response variable is diagnosis, which indicates whether each tumor is benign or malignant. The dataset also contains 30 numeric features describing characteristics of cell nuclei from tumor samples, such as radius, texture, perimeter, area, smoothness, compactness, concavity and many more.

We will:

  • train the models introduced in the lecture on a training set
  • evaluate their performance on a test set
  • compare different classifiers.

Preparation

Before fitting any models, we first load the dataset and inspect its structure.

  1. Load the packages needed for this practical.

    We will use packages for tree-based methods, Support Vector Machines, model evaluation, and data handling.

    Hint: Use library() to load the required packages.

Show Answer 
library(tree)
library(randomForest)
library(xgboost)
library(e1071)
library(caret)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)


  1. We will use 75% of the observations as the training set and the remaining 25% as the test set. Create a vector containing the row indices of the observations that will be used for training. Use sample() and set the seed to 1 for reproducibility.

    Hint: Use set.seed() before sample(). The function nrow(tumor) gives the number of observations in the dataset.

Show Answer 
# Setting a seed ensures the random train/test split is identical every time the code runs
set.seed(1)

# Randomly select 75% of the observations for the training set
train <- sample(1:nrow(tumor), size = 0.75 * nrow(tumor))


Model training

In this section, we train the classifiers on the training set. We also create plots that help us understand how these classifiers work.

The models are fitted using only the training observations selected in the previous section. Later, we will evaluate the fitted models on the test set.

Pruned tree

A decision tree can easily overfit the training data if it grows too large. This means that the tree may fit the training data very well, but perform worse on new data.

Pruning reduces the size of the tree by removing splits that do not improve predictive performance. In this practical, we use cross-validation to choose an appropriate tree size.

  1. Obtain a pruned tree for the training set. Save the object as tumor_prune, and plot it.

    Hint: Use tree() to grow the initial tree, cv.tree() to find the optimal size via cross-validation, and prune.tree() to cut it back.

Show Answer 
# make a tree object that is, Fit a classification tree on the training data
tumor_tree  <- tree(diagnosis ~ ., data = tumor[train, ])
# or this tumor_tree <- tree(diagnosis ~ ., data = tumor, subset = train)
# Perform cross-validation to select tree size
cv_tumor    <- cv.tree(tumor_tree)

# Select the tree with the lowest cross-validated deviance
tumor_prune <- prune.tree(tumor_tree, best = cv_tumor$size[which.min(cv_tumor$dev)])

## or This chooses the tree size with the lowest cross-validated classification error.
# cv_tumor <- cv.tree(tumor_tree, FUN = prune.misclass)
# tumor_prune <- prune.misclass(tumor_tree, best = cv_tumor$size[which.min(cv_tumor$dev)])

# plot the pruned tree
plot(tumor_prune)
text(tumor_prune, cex = 0.8)


Bagging and Random Forest

Single decision trees often have high variance, meaning their predictions can change a lot with small changes in the data.

Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) reduces variance by training many trees on bootstrap samples of the training data. For classification problems, the trees are combined using a majority vote.

Random forests further improve this idea by using a random subset of predictors at each split. This makes the trees less correlated and can improve predictive performance.

  1. Train the bagging model tumor_bag and the random forest model tumor_rf on the training set. Display the output of both models. Set the seed to 1 for reproducibility.

    Hint: Bagging uses all predictors at each split, so set mtry equal to the number of predictors. Random forests use a random subset of predictors at each split. Use randomForest(). The default mtry for classification in randomForest() is floor(sqrt(p)). Since there are 30 predictors, the default is 5.

Show Answer 
set.seed(1)

# Bagging: use all 30 predictors at each split
tumor_bag <- randomForest(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = tumor[train, ],
  importance = TRUE,
  mtry = 30,
  ntree = 250
)

tumor_bag

    The importance measure shows how much the prediction accuracy decreases when a variable is permuted. Variables that cause a larger decrease in accuracy are considered more important for the model.

    Hint: Use varImpPlot(). The argument n.var = 10 displays the 10 most important predictors, and type = 1 uses the mean decrease in accuracy.*

Boosting

The previous models used either one tree or many independent trees. Boosting is another ensemble method, but it works differently from bagging and random forests.

Boosting builds trees sequentially. Each new tree tries to improve the mistakes made by the previous trees. The final prediction is obtained by combining many small trees, which often improves predictive accuracy.

In this practical, we use the xgboost package to fit a boosted tree model.

Preparing the data for XGBoost

  1. Prepare the training data for xgboost.

    The xgboost package requires the predictors to be stored in a numeric matrix and the response variable to be coded as 0 and 1.

    Use the training observations only. Convert diagnosis into a binary response, where:

  • 0 means benign;

  • 1 means malignant.

    Then use model.matrix() to create a numeric matrix of predictors and use xgb.DMatrix() to create the training object.

    Hint: Use tumor[train, ] to select the training data. Use ifelse() to convert diagnosis into 0/1 values. Use model.matrix(diagnosis ~ . - 1, data = tumor_train) to create the predictor matrix.

Show Answer 
# Training data
tumor_train <- tumor[train, ]

# Make sure diagnosis is a factor
tumor_train$diagnosis <- as.factor(tumor_train$diagnosis)

# Convert the response variable to 0/1
# Benign = 0, Malignant = 1
y <- ifelse(tumor_train$diagnosis == "M", 1, 0)

# Convert predictors to a numeric matrix
x <- model.matrix(diagnosis ~ . - 1, data = tumor_train)

## Create the XGBoost training matrix. That is, XGBoost training object, 
## which stores the predictors and labels

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x, label = y)


Tuning the XGBoost model

  1. Use 5-fold cross-validation to compare several XGBoost tuning combinations.

    We vary the following hyperparameters:

  • eta: the learning rate. It controls how strongly each new tree contributes to the model. Smaller values make learning slower but can sometimes improve generalization.

  • max_depth: the maximum depth of each tree;

  • colsample_bytree: the proportion of predictors sampled for each tree;

  • subsample: the proportion of observations sampled for each tree.

    We also set:

  • gamma = 0: it says allow a split if it gives any improvement. No extra restriction is added for making a split. Larger values make the model more conservative.

  • min_child_weight = 1: the default value. Larger values make it harder to create very small leaves and can reduce overfitting to some extent.

    Use classification error as the evaluation metric. Then calculate accuracy as 1 - error.

    Hint: Use expand.grid() to create a data frame containing all combinations of the tuning parameter values. Each row of this grid is one combination of hyperparameter values that will be tested. Then use createFolds(tumor_train$diagnosis, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE) to create the same 5 test folds for all tuning combinations. Inside the for loop, take one row of the grid at a time, put those values into a list called xgb_params, and pass them to xgb.cv(). The output cv$evaluation_log contains the cross-validation error for each boosting round. Use which.min(eval_log$test_error_mean) to find the boosting round with the lowest cross-validated error. Store the error and calculate accuracy using 1 - error.

Show Answer 
dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x, label = y)
# Grid search over learning rate, tree depth, and stochastic sampling parameters
xgb_grid <- expand.grid(
  eta = c(0.3, 0.4),
  max_depth = c(1, 2, 3),
  gamma = 0,
  colsample_bytree = c(0.6, 0.8),
  min_child_weight = 1,
  subsample = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.0),
  nrounds = 100
)

# Create the same 5 folds for all tuning combinations
set.seed(1)
folds <- createFolds(tumor_train$diagnosis, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

# Store cross-validation results
cv_results <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(xgb_grid))) {
  
  # Define parameters for this tuning combination
  xgb_params <- list(
    objective = "binary:logistic",
    eval_metric = "error",
    eta = xgb_grid$eta[i],
    max_depth = xgb_grid$max_depth[i],
    gamma = xgb_grid$gamma[i],
    colsample_bytree = xgb_grid$colsample_bytree[i],
    min_child_weight = xgb_grid$min_child_weight[i],
    subsample = xgb_grid$subsample[i],
    seed = 1,
    verbosity = 0
  )
  
  # 5-fold cross-validation
  cv <- xgb.cv(
    params = xgb_params,
    data = dtrain,
    nrounds = xgb_grid$nrounds[i],
    folds = folds,
    verbose = 0
  )
  
  # Extract cross-validation results
  eval_log <- cv$evaluation_log
  
  # Select the number of boosting rounds with the lowest test error
  best_idx <- which.min(eval_log$test_error_mean)
  
  # Save the results
  cv_results[[i]] <- data.frame(
    eta = xgb_grid$eta[i],
    max_depth = xgb_grid$max_depth[i],
    gamma = xgb_grid$gamma[i],
    colsample_bytree = xgb_grid$colsample_bytree[i],
    min_child_weight = xgb_grid$min_child_weight[i],
    subsample = xgb_grid$subsample[i],
    best_iteration = eval_log$iter[best_idx],
    error = eval_log$test_error_mean[best_idx],
    accuracy = 1 - eval_log$test_error_mean[best_idx]
  )
}

# Combine all cross-validation results
xgb_tuning_results <- bind_rows(cv_results)

# Display the tuning results
xgb_tuning_results

Fitting the final XGBoost model

  1. Select the tuning combination with the highest cross-validated accuracy. Then fit the final boosted tree model and save it as tumor_xgb.

    Hint: The object xgb_tuning_results contains one row for each tuning combination tested in cross-validation. First, sort this table by accuracy from highest to lowest using arrange(desc(accuracy)). Then use slice(1) to keep only the best row and save it as best_params_row. The values in best_params_row are used to define the final XGBoost parameters. Finally, use xgb.train() to fit the final model on the full training data dtrain. Use best_params_row$best_iteration as the value of nrounds, because this is the number of boosting rounds that gave the lowest cross-validated error.

Show Answer 
dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x, label = y)
# Select the tuning combination with the highest accuracy
best_params_row <- xgb_tuning_results %>%
  arrange(desc(accuracy)) %>%
  slice(1)

best_params_row
##   eta max_depth gamma colsample_bytree min_child_weight subsample
## 1 0.4         3     0              0.8                1         1
##   best_iteration      error  accuracy
## 1             67 0.02344733 0.9765527
# Define the final model parameters
final_params <- list(
  objective = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric = "error",
  eta = best_params_row$eta,
  max_depth = best_params_row$max_depth,
  gamma = best_params_row$gamma,
  colsample_bytree = best_params_row$colsample_bytree,
  min_child_weight = best_params_row$min_child_weight,
  subsample = best_params_row$subsample,
  seed = 1,
  verbosity = 0
)

# Fit the final XGBoost model
tumor_xgb <- xgb.train(
  params = final_params,
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = best_params_row$best_iteration,
  verbose = 0
)

tumor_xgb
## ##### xgb.Booster
## call:
##   xgb.train(params = final_params, data = dtrain, nrounds = best_params_row$best_iteration, 
##     verbose = 0)
## # of features: 30 
## # of rounds:  67

The object tumor_xgb is the final fitted boosted tree model.It has learned patterns from the training data and can later be used to predict whether tumors in the test set are benign or malignant. The model uses 30 features, corresponding to the 30 numeric predictors in the tumor dataset.The model was trained for 67 boosting rounds. This number was selected from cross-validation as the number of rounds with the lowest cross-validated classification error.


  1. Plot the cross-validation results to examine how the tuning parameters affect model performance. The plot shows the cross-validated accuracy for different combinations of max_depth, eta, subsample, and colsample_bytree. Higher accuracy indicates better performance.

    Hint: Use ggplot() with max_depth on the x-axis and accuracy on the y-axis. Use different colors for different values of eta, and use facets to compare different values of subsample and colsample_bytree. Note that colsample_bytree the proportion of predictors randomly selected when building each tree. Smaller values make the trees more different from each other and may help reduce overfitting.

Show Answer 
# Visualizing the hyperparameter landscape helps confirm if the model is stable across different settings
ggplot(
  xgb_tuning_results,
  aes(
    x = factor(max_depth),
    y = accuracy,
    color = factor(eta),
    group = factor(eta)
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(
    subsample ~ colsample_bytree,
    labeller = label_both
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Max depth",
    y = "Cross-validated accuracy",
    color = "Eta",
    title = "XGBoost tuning results",
    subtitle = "Higher accuracy is better"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


Question: Which combination of tuning parameters gives the highest cross-validated accuracy?

Question: Does increasing max_depth always improve the cross-validated accuracy? What does this tell us about model complexity?

The plot shows the cross-validated accuracy for different XGBoost tuning combinations.

So, all tuning combinations perform well, with cross-validated accuracy roughly between 0.962 and 0.977. This means that XGBoost is relatively stable on this dataset: changing the tuning parameters changes the accuracy only slightly.

The best-performing model has eta = 0.4, max_depth = 3, colsample_bytree = 0.8, and subsample = 1. This model has a cross-validated accuracy of approximately 0.977.

There is no clear pattern showing that larger max_depth always improves performance. In some cases, deeper trees perform better, but in other cases they perform worse. This shows that increasing model complexity does not always improve predictive performance.

The effect of eta also depends on the other tuning parameters. Sometimes eta = 0.4 performs better, while in other settings eta = 0.3 performs similarly or only slightly worse.

The plot suggests that the XGBoost model performs well, but the exact choice of tuning parameters has only a small effect on cross-validated accuracy. We will still evaluate the final model on the test set before making a final conclusion.

  1. Identify the tuning combination with the highest cross-validated accuracy.

    Note that in this code arrange(desc(accuracy)) sorts the results from highest to lowest accuracy. Then slice(1) keeps only the best row.

    Hint: arrange(desc(accuracy)) sorts the results from highest to lowest accuracy, and slice(1) keeps only the top row.

Question: Which tuning combination gives the highest cross-validated accuracy? What is the value of that accuracy?

  1. Display the variable importance plot for the final XGBoost model.

    As you know, variable importance helps us understand which predictors were most useful for the XGBoost model. In xgboost, the default importance measure is Gain, which shows how much each variable contributed to improving the model when it was used in a split.

    Hint: First use xgb.importance() to calculate the importance values. The argument feature_names = colnames(x) gives the predictor names, and model = tumor_xgb tells R to use the final fitted XGBoost model. Then use xgb.plot.importance() to plot the most important predictors. The argument top_n = 20 shows only the 20 most important variables, which makes the plot easier to read.

Show Answer 
# Gain measures the improvement in accuracy brought by a feature to the branches it is on.
importance_matrix <- xgb.importance(
  feature_names = colnames(x),
  model = tumor_xgb
)

importance_matrix

Question: Which predictors are most important in the final XGBoost model? Are they similar to the important predictors found for bagging and random forest?

The variable importance plot shows which predictors contributed most to the final XGBoost model.

The most important predictor is concave_points_mean. It has a much larger importance value than all other predictors, meaning that it contributed the most to improving the model’s classification performance. The next most important predictors are concave_points_worst, perimeter_worst, and texture_worst. These variables also helped the model distinguish between benign and malignant tumors, but their importance is much smaller than that of concave_points_mean. Most of the remaining variables have relatively low importance. This suggests that the XGBoost model relies mainly on a small number of highly informative predictors.

So, the plot suggests that variables related to concave points, perimeter, texture, area, and radius are especially useful for classifying tumors as benign or malignant.

Support Vector Machines (SVM)

As we learned in the lecture, SVMs classify observations by finding a boundary that separates the classes as well as possible.

With a linear kernel, the decision boundary is linear. With a radial kernel, the decision boundary can be nonlinear, allowing the model to capture more complex patterns in the data.

SVMs are sensitive to the scale of the predictors. Therefore, the predictors should be scaled before fitting the model. The function tune.svm() scales the predictors by default.

  1. Train an SVM model with a radial kernel on the training set. Tune the cost parameter and save the result as tumor_svm_radial. Then train an SVM model with a linear kernel using the same cost values and save the result as tumor_svm_linear.

    Hint: Use tune.svm(). The argument kernel = "radial" fits a nonlinear SVM, while kernel = "linear" fits a linear SVM. The argument cost controls the penalty for classification mistakes.

Show Answer 
set.seed(1)

# Tuning the radial kernel SVM: finding the optimal cost (C) parameter to balance margin width and training errors
tumor_svm_radial <- tune.svm(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = tumor[train, ],
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = c(0.5, 1, 1.5),
  tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 5)
)

tumor_svm_radial
## 
## Parameter tuning of 'svm':
## 
## - sampling method: 5-fold cross validation 
## 
## - best parameters:
##  cost
##   1.5
## 
## - best performance: 0.02350205
set.seed(1)

# Tuning the linear kernel SVM: assessing if a simple straight hyper-plane is sufficient
tumor_svm_linear <- tune.svm(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = tumor[train, ],
  kernel = "linear",
  cost = c(0.5, 1, 1.5),
  tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 5)
)

tumor_svm_linear
## 
## Parameter tuning of 'svm':
## 
## - sampling method: 5-fold cross validation 
## 
## - best parameters:
##  cost
##   0.5
## 
## - best performance: 0.02112175

The tuning output shows the best value of cost for each SVM model and the corresponding cross-validation error.

For the radial SVM, the best value is cost = 1, with a cross-validation error of approximately 0.024.

For the linear SVM, the best value is cost = 0.5, with a cross-validation error of approximately 0.021.

Since the linear SVM has the lower cross-validation error, it performs slightly better than the radial SVM on the training data during cross-validation.

The difference between the two errors is small, so both kernels perform well.

However, based on cross-validation, the linear kernel is preferred here.

Note that The tuning parameter cost controls the trade-off between allowing classification errors and fitting the training data closely. - A smaller cost allows more training errors and usually gives a simpler model. - A larger cost penalizes training errors more strongly and may give a more complex model. We tune cost to find the value that gives the lowest cross-validation error.


Question: Which kernel gives the lower cross-validation error: the radial kernel or the linear kernel?

Testing the models

In this section, we evaluate the fitted models on the test set. The test set contains the observations that were not used for training.

  1. Save the class predictions of all fitted models on the test set.

    Hint: Use tumor[-train, ] to select the test observations. For most models, use predict() directly. For XGBoost, first create the test predictor matrix in the same format as the training predictor matrix.

Show Answer 
# Test data
tumor_test <- tumor[-train, ]

# Pruned tree predictions
prune <- predict(
  tumor_prune,
  newdata = tumor_test,
  type = "class"
)

# Bagging predictions
bag <- predict(
  tumor_bag,
  newdata = tumor_test
)

# Random forest predictions
rf <- predict(
  tumor_rf,
  newdata = tumor_test
)

# XGBoost needs the test predictors in the same model.matrix format as training
test_x <- model.matrix(diagnosis ~ . - 1, data = tumor_test)
test_x <- test_x[, colnames(x), drop = FALSE]

# Predicted probabilities for the malignant class
boost_prob <- predict(tumor_xgb, test_x)

# Convert probabilities to class labels
boost <- ifelse(
  boost_prob > 0.5,
  "M",
  "B"
)

boost <- factor(boost, levels = levels(tumor$diagnosis))

# Radial SVM predictions
svm_radial <- predict(
  tumor_svm_radial$best.model,
  newdata = tumor_test
)

# Linear SVM predictions
svm_linear <- predict(
  tumor_svm_linear$best.model,
  newdata = tumor_test
)

Advanced exercise

  1. Display boxplots of the standardized features and of the standardized logarithms of the features.

    This exercise helps us see how the distributions of the predictors change after applying a logarithmic transformation. The logarithmic transformation can reduce the effect of very large values and make skewed variables look more symmetric.

    Hint: Use tumor[, -1] to remove the response variable diagnosis. Use scale() to standardize the predictors so that they have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Use log() before scale() to standardize the logarithms of the predictors.

Show Answer 
# Visualizing the impact of log transformations on feature scale and skewness
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

boxplot(
  scale(tumor[, -1]),
  main = "Standardized features",
  las = 2
)

boxplot(
  scale(log(tumor[, -1]+1)),
  main = "Standardized log-features",
  las = 2
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The left plot shows the standardized original features. Several variables have many large positive outliers, with some standardized values above 10. This suggests that some predictors are strongly right-skewed.

The right plot shows the standardized logarithms of the features. After applying the logarithmic transformation, the distributions are more balanced around zero, and the most extreme positive values are reduced. The outliers are still present, but they are less extreme than in the original standardized features.

So, the logarithmic transformation reduces skewness and makes the feature distributions more comparable. This can be useful for methods such as SVMs, which are sensitive to the scale and distribution of the predictors.


Question: How do the boxplots change after applying the logarithmic transformation? Which version appears to have fewer extreme values?

  1. Create a new dataset with log-transformed numeric features.

    We now repeat the model comparison using log-transformed predictors. This allows us to check whether reducing skewness in the predictors improves model performance.

    Hint: Use mutate() with across(where(is.numeric), ...) to apply the same transformation to all numeric predictors. We use log(x + 1) to avoid problems if any feature contains zero.

Show Answer 
# Safely applying log(x+1) to all numeric columns to prevent log(0) -Inf errors
ltumor <- tumor %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ log(.x + 1))) %>%
  as.data.frame()

ltumor$diagnosis <- as.factor(ltumor$diagnosis)

# Training and test sets for the log-transformed data
ltumor_train <- ltumor[train, ]
ltumor_test  <- ltumor[-train, ]


  1. Train the same models using the log-transformed features.

    Train a pruned tree, bagging model, random forest, XGBoost model, radial SVM, and linear SVM using the log-transformed training set.

    Hint: Use the same modelling functions as before, but replace tumor with ltumor. For XGBoost, create new objects such as lx, ly, and ldtrain so that we do not overwrite the objects used for the original features.

Show Answer 
## Pruned tree
ltumor_tree <- tree(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = ltumor_train
)

cv_ltumor <- cv.tree(ltumor_tree)

ltumor_prune <- prune.tree(
  ltumor_tree,
  best = cv_ltumor$size[which.min(cv_ltumor$dev)]
)

## Bagging
set.seed(1)
ltumor_bag <- randomForest(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = ltumor_train,
  importance = TRUE,
  mtry = 30,
  ntree = 250
)

## Random forest
set.seed(1)
ltumor_rf <- randomForest(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = ltumor_train,
  importance = TRUE,
  ntree = 250
)

## XGBoost preparation
ltumor_train$diagnosis <- as.factor(ltumor_train$diagnosis)

ly <- ifelse(ltumor_train$diagnosis == "M", 1, 0)

lx <- model.matrix(diagnosis ~ . - 1, data = ltumor_train)

ldtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = lx, label = ly)

## XGBoost tuning grid
lxgb_grid <- expand.grid(
  eta = c(0.3, 0.4),
  max_depth = c(1, 2, 3),
  gamma = 0,
  colsample_bytree = c(0.6, 0.8),
  min_child_weight = 1,
  subsample = c(0.5, 0.75, 1.0),
  nrounds = 100
)

# Create the same 5 folds for all XGBoost tuning combinations
set.seed(1)
lfolds <- createFolds(ltumor_train$diagnosis, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

lcv_results <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(lxgb_grid))) {
  
  lxgb_params <- list(
    objective = "binary:logistic",
    eval_metric = "error",
    eta = lxgb_grid$eta[i],
    max_depth = lxgb_grid$max_depth[i],
    gamma = lxgb_grid$gamma[i],
    colsample_bytree = lxgb_grid$colsample_bytree[i],
    min_child_weight = lxgb_grid$min_child_weight[i],
    subsample = lxgb_grid$subsample[i],
    seed = 1,
    verbosity = 0
  )
  
  lcv <- xgb.cv(
    params = lxgb_params,
    data = ldtrain,
    nrounds = lxgb_grid$nrounds[i],
    folds = lfolds,
    verbose = 0
  )
  
  leval_log <- lcv$evaluation_log
  lbest_idx <- which.min(leval_log$test_error_mean)
  
  lcv_results[[i]] <- data.frame(
    eta = lxgb_grid$eta[i],
    max_depth = lxgb_grid$max_depth[i],
    gamma = lxgb_grid$gamma[i],
    colsample_bytree = lxgb_grid$colsample_bytree[i],
    min_child_weight = lxgb_grid$min_child_weight[i],
    subsample = lxgb_grid$subsample[i],
    best_iteration = leval_log$iter[lbest_idx],
    error = leval_log$test_error_mean[lbest_idx],
    accuracy = 1 - leval_log$test_error_mean[lbest_idx]
  )
}

ltumor_xgb_tuning_results <- bind_rows(lcv_results)

ltumor_best_params_row <- ltumor_xgb_tuning_results %>%
  arrange(desc(accuracy)) %>%
  slice(1)

lfinal_params <- list(
  objective = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric = "error",
  eta = ltumor_best_params_row$eta,
  max_depth = ltumor_best_params_row$max_depth,
  gamma = ltumor_best_params_row$gamma,
  colsample_bytree = ltumor_best_params_row$colsample_bytree,
  min_child_weight = ltumor_best_params_row$min_child_weight,
  subsample = ltumor_best_params_row$subsample,
  seed = 1,
  verbosity = 0
)

ltumor_xgb <- xgb.train(
  params = lfinal_params,
  data = ldtrain,
  nrounds = ltumor_best_params_row$best_iteration,
  verbose = 0
)

## Radial SVM
set.seed(1)
ltumor_svm_radial <- tune.svm(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = ltumor_train,
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = c(0.5, 1, 1.5),
  gamma = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1),
  tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 5)
)

## Linear SVM
set.seed(1)
ltumor_svm_linear <- tune.svm(
  diagnosis ~ .,
  data = ltumor_train,
  kernel = "linear",
  cost = c(0.5, 1, 1.5),
  tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 5)
)

## 1   Pruned tree Log-transformed            19 0.8671329
## 2       Bagging Log-transformed            11 0.9230769
## 3 Random forest Log-transformed             7 0.9510490
## 4      Boosting Log-transformed             5 0.9650350
## 5    SVM radial Log-transformed             4 0.9720280
## 6    SVM linear Log-transformed             4 0.9720280

The results show that the log-transformed features give different test-set performance across the models.

The pruned tree performs the worst, with 19 misclassified observations and an accuracy of about 0.867. Most of its errors are malignant tumors predicted as benign, which is an important type of error in this classification problem.

The tree ensemble methods perform better than the single pruned tree. Bagging misclassifies 11 observations, random forest misclassifies 8 observations, and boosting misclassifies only 5 observations.

The best performance is obtained by the SVM models. Both the radial SVM and the linear SVM misclassify only 4 observations, giving a test accuracy of about 0.972.

For the radial SVM, there is 1 benign tumor predicted as malignant and 3 malignant tumors predicted as benign. For the linear SVM, there are 2 benign tumors predicted as malignant and 2 malignant tumors predicted as benign.

So, after applying the log transformation, the SVM models perform best on the test set. The log transformation seems especially useful for SVMs, which are sensitive to the scale and distribution of predictors. So, The radial SVM and linear SVM have the fewest misclassified observations, with 4 errors each. Therefore, they are the best-performing models among the log-transformed-feature models. Their test accuracy is approximately 0.972.


Question: Did the log transformation improve test-set performance? Which model has the fewest misclassified observations after the log transformation?

Answer: After the log transformation, the best-performing models are the radial SVM and the linear SVM, both with 4 misclassified observations and a test accuracy of approximately 0.972. Boosting is the best-performing tree-based method after the log transformation, with 5 misclassified observations and a test accuracy of approximately 0.965.

To decide whether the log transformation improved performance, we need to compare these results with the corresponding results from the models trained on the original features. So, if you still have time, you can do it right now. Otherwise, please do not forget to do that at home.

Conclusion

In this practical, we applied several supervised learning methods to classify tumors as benign or malignant using the tumor dataset.

We trained and compared the following models:

  • Pruned decision tree
  • Bagging
  • Random forest
  • Boosting (XGBoost)
  • Support Vector Machines (linear and radial SVMs)

The results show that a single decision tree can have weaker predictive performance than more advanced methods. Pruning helps control the complexity of the tree, but the tree-based ensemble methods generally performed better.

Ensemble methods such as bagging, random forests, and boosting combine many trees. This often improves predictive performance compared with a single tree. In this practical, boosting was the best-performing tree-based method.

The SVM models provided another powerful classification approach. We compared both a linear kernel and a radial kernel. This comparison showed that a more flexible nonlinear boundary is not always necessary; in this dataset, the linear SVM performed very well.

Finally, we evaluated all models on a test set using confusion matrices, the number of misclassified observations, and test accuracy. We also explored how log-transforming the predictors can influence model performance.

So, this practical illustrates how different machine learning methods can be applied to the same classification problem, and how their predictive performance may differ depending on the model complexity, tuning parameters, and data transformation.

End of lab
